Efficient Penalty-Based Bilevel Methods: Improved Analysis, Novel Updates, and Flatness Condition

Liuyuan Jiang, Quan Xiao, Lisha Chen, Tianyi Chen

Efficient penalty methods / The takeaway

Reduce the work inside a bilevel training step.

Repeated inner solves can dominate the cost of bilevel training. This paper sharpens the curvature analysis to allow larger outer steps and removes one response computation when the outer objective changes little near a lower-level optimum. Fixed constraints admit one update per level. When the constraints move with the outer decision, the method retains a constrained inner solve.

Curvature analysisStable outer step sizes

Under the analyzed regularity conditions, the curvature bound after lower-level optimization stays bounded as the penalty grows.

↘Fixed constraintsOne update per level

The PBGD-Free variant tracks the lower variable once, then updates the upper variable. Flatness controls the bias from the removed correction.

Related paper · NeurIPS 2025

Beyond Value Functions: Single-Loop Bilevel Optimization under Flatness Conditions

PBGD-Free develops value-function removal under flatness. This preprint expands the smoothness analysis and develops fixed-set and coupled-constraint updates.

01The idea

Separate the sources of cost in a penalty method.

The decision

A bilevel learner chooses an outer variable while its inner variable solves another objective. A penalty makes inner suboptimality costly, but the chosen formulation and the update schedule determine which computation is actually required.

The bottleneck

There are three distinct costs: a penalty-scaled step-size restriction, two lower-level response estimates, and the extra structure of constraints that move with the outer decision. Treating them as one difficulty obscures which improvement applies.

The idea

Analyze the reduced objective to capture curvature cancellation, then alternate lower responses and outer updates. Upper-level flatness controls the bias from removing a value-function correction. The coupled extension incorporates constraint multipliers and boundary regularity.

1

The surface is a joint gradient

Changing x at an arbitrary fixed y can amplify the penalty contribution. That is the geometry seen by a generic joint update.

2

The line follows the inner response

The reduced gradient first accounts for lower-level optimization. The paper’s example shows far less variation along this response as the penalty increases.

3

Curvature along the optimized response

The example shows how following the optimized lower response changes the gradient’s dependence on the penalty. The reduced-smoothness theorems formalize that mechanism for their constraint regimes.

How the method works

  1. 01

    Analyze the reduced objective

    Analyze curvature along the optimized lower-level response to obtain a penalty-independent smoothness order.

  2. 02

    Use upper-level flatness

    Control the effect of dropping the value-function correction when the stated flatness condition holds.

  3. 03

    Account for constraints

    Distinguish fixed lower-level domains from feasible sets that move with the outer variable.

Efficiency has more than one bottleneck

Outer step size, value-function response tracking, and coupled-constraint solves contribute separately to the computation. The paper gives a smoothness analysis and update rules for each constraint regime.

In practice

Preference learning and constrained classifiers

In LLM adaptation, flatness supports preference learning in a backbone with a supervised head. In constrained SVMs, outer violation bounds reshape the inner feasible set. The fixed-set and coupled algorithms address these different response structures.

Result

Reduced smoothness and value-function removal are separate gains. The fixed-set PBGD-Free analysis covers a fully single-loop update; the coupled extension removes one response computation and still pays for the remaining constrained solve.

Experiment setup and comparison details

Theorem 3.1 treats fixed-set reduced smoothness; Theorem 5.1 treats coupled smoothness under Assumptions 1–5, including strict complementarity and boundary regularity. Theorems 4.1 and 5.2 analyze the corresponding PBGD-Free variants under flatness.

The inner solve with coupled constraints

The fixed-set PBGD-Free method is fully single-loop. With coupled constraints, it retains a constrained inner solve, which contributes to the total complexity alongside the outer iterations.

Theorems 3.1 and 5.1

Curvature cancellation survives constraints

The scaled difference of nearby value functions admits a penalty-independent smoothness order under the theorem-specific regularity. Directional derivatives are analytical tools; the implementation still uses first-order information.

Read the statement ↗
Theorems 4.1 and 5.2

Flatness controls a residual

The flatness residual controls the stationarity neighborhood in both results. The fixed-set theorem uses the reduced objective. The coupled theorem measures stationarity of its multiplier-dependent surrogate and retains an inner solve.

Read the statement ↗
Reasoning behind the formulation

Cancellation changes the smoothness analysis

FγF_\gammaFγ​ = γ\gammaγ(vγv_\gammavγ​ − v) is built from nearby value functions. Their directional curvature terms can cancel. Theorem 3.1 establishes O(1)\mathcal O(1)O(1) reduced smoothness with fixed constraints; Theorem 5.1 extends it under Assumptions 1–5 for coupled constraints.

Flatness changes which correction is necessary

Upper-level flatness controls the objective’s sensitivity to lower-level deviations. That structure bounds the bias from omitting the value-function contribution in PBGD-Free.

Coupled constraints change the remaining work

When c(x, y) depends on x, multipliers enter the value-function derivative. The coupled PBGD-Free method retains an inner loop to estimate the constrained response.

Assumptions behind the analysis

Theorems 3.1 and 5.1 establish reduced smoothness. Theorems 4.1 and 5.2 analyze PBGD-Free under flatness, with a fully single-loop fixed-set update and a retained inner solve for coupled constraints. The coupled results use bounded multipliers, strict complementarity, and boundary regularity.

Questions

How does this relate to the conference papers?

It is a broader preprint developing the smoothness analysis and flatness-based updates together. The EUSIPCO page focuses on reduced curvature; the NeurIPS 2025 page focuses on value-function removal under flatness.

What role does flatness play in removing the correction?

Flatness controls upper-objective sensitivity near a lower-level optimum and bounds the bias from omission. The paper’s counterexample motivates this condition by showing a persistent error with the simplified outer partial gradient.

Related projects

This preprint extends the value-function removal developed in the NeurIPS 2025 PBGD-Free paper. The EUSIPCO 2025 paper establishes the sharper reduced-smoothness analysis.
